 1                                           INTRODUCTION

 2          The principal basis for Plaintiff Epicrew USA’s (“Epicrew”) complaint is that, allegedly,

 3   Defendant Capital Asset Exchange & Trading LLC (“CAET”) told Epicrew that CAET owned

 4   certain semiconductor equipment that Epicrew agreed to purchase from CAET (the

 5   “Equipment”), when in fact CAET did not own the Equipment, and Epicrew would not have

 6   entered into its contracts with CAET had it known that fact. However, this claim is contrary to

 7   language in the contracts that the complaint itself acknowledges. Both contracts, which were

 8   called “Invoice Orders,” stated that “[a]ll Equipment is offered to Buyer,” i.e., Epicrew, “based

 9   on its prior sale to CAET. Should such prior sale not occur, this invoice shall be null and void.”

10   (Decl. of William J. Frimel in Supp. of Mot. to Dismiss, Jul. 17, 2024 (“Frimel Decl.”), Exh. A, ¶

11   5; id. Exh. B, ¶ 5.) The orders also required Epicrew to agree “not to circumvent CAET by

12   purchasing [the] Equipment directly from CAET’s supplier.” (Id. Exh. A, ¶ 4; id. Exh. B, ¶ 4.)

13   In other words, the Invoice Orders acknowledged the possibility that CAET might not yet own

14   the Equipment, as CAET’s supplier might not yet have sold it to CAET. The reason for this, as

15   communications between the parties that Epicrew also cites reflect, is that CAET functions as an

16   intermediary between buyers and sellers of semiconductor equipment. Regardless, Epicrew fails

17   to identify any alleged statement by CAET to the effect that CAET owned the Equipment. Thus,

18   Epicrew’s complaint fails to state a claim, and must be dismissed under Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6).

19          First, Epicrew alleges numerous causes of action that sound in fraud, including fraud,

20   negligent misrepresentation, intentional misrepresentation, “concealment” and “false promise.”
21   The first four such claims (i.e., Epicrew’s Third, Fourth, Fifth and Sixth Causes of Action) are

22   based on CAET’s purported representation that it owned the Equipment, which supposedly

23   induced Epicrew to enter into the Invoice Orders. As discussed, however, the complaint fails to

24   identify any statement by CAET indicating that it owned the Equipment, or who at CAET made

25   that statement, and thus does not plead fraud with particularity as required by Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b).

26   See Kearns v. Ford Motor Co., 567 F.3d 1120, 1126 (9th Cir. 2009) (complaint “failed to plead . .
27   . fraud with particularity” because “[n]owhere . . . does [plaintiff] specify what [defendant’s]

28   television advertisements or other sales material specifically stated”). Further, the Invoice Orders

                                                   MEM. OF PS. & AS. IN SUPP. OF DEF.’S MOT. TO DISMISS
        Case 5:24-cv-03676-EJD Document 13 Filed 07/17/24 Page 9 of 28



 1   expressly acknowledged that CAET might not own the Equipment at the time Epicrew executed

 2   the orders, and thus Epicrew could not have reasonably relied on any statement by CAET to the

 3   effect that it owned the Equipment in any event. See Baymiller v. Guarantee Mut. Life Co., No.

 4   SA CV99-1566, 2000 WL 33774562, *4 (C.D. Cal. Aug. 3, 2000) (dismissing fraud claim

 5   because “there cannot be reasonable reliance upon misrepresentations . . . that are contradicted by

 6   the express language of the insurance contracts”). In addition, as Epicrew’s fraud claims seek the

 7   same relief as its breach of contract claims — i.e., the return of Epicrew’s payment for the

 8   Equipment — and are based on CAET’s alleged breach of its contractual obligation to deliver the

 9   Equipment, Epicrew’s fraud claims are barred by the economic loss rule. See JMP Secs. LLP v.

10   Altair Nanotechnologies, Inc., 880 F. Supp. 2d 1029, 1043 (N.D. Cal. 2012) (as plaintiff’s “fraud

11   and negligent misrepresentation . . . . claims consist of nothing more than [defendant’s] alleged

12   failure to make good on its contractual promises,” “both claims are barred by California’s

13   economic loss rule”).

14          Likewise, Epicrew’s Seventh Cause of Action for “false promise,” or promissory fraud,

15   merely reiterates Epicrew’s breach of contract claim — i.e., that CAET failed to deliver the

16   Equipment as promised — and is hence barred by the economic loss rule as well. This claim

17   must also be dismissed because Epicrew does not allege, with particularity, any facts indicating

18   that CAET never intended to provide the Equipment to Epicrew.

19          Second, Epicrew asserts claims for breach of contract and of the implied covenant of good

20   faith and fair dealing (its First and Second Causes of Action). According to the complaint, CAET
21   breached the Invoice Orders by failing to deliver the Equipment “in a timely manner.” However,

22   Epicrew identifies no provision of the Invoice Orders requiring delivery “in a timely manner,” or

23   defining what constitutes timely delivery under those agreements. Thus, Epicrew does not state a

24   claim for breach of contract. See Young v. Facebook, Inc., 790 F. Supp. 2d 1110, 1117 (N.D. Cal.

25   2011) (“In an action for breach of a written contract, a plaintiff must allege the specific provisions

26   in the contract creating the obligation the defendant is said to have breached.”). Epicrew’s
27   implied covenant cause of action simply incorporates by reference Epicrew’s allegations

28   elsewhere in the complaint, which fail to state a cognizable claim.

 1          Third, Epicrew alleges claims under Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200 and for declaratory

 2   relief (its Eighth and Ninth Causes of Action). Epicrew’s Section 17200 claim relies on (1)

 3   CAET’s supposed representation that it owned the Equipment, which is inadequately pleaded for

 4   the reasons discussed; and (2) CAET’s alleged refusal to give Epicrew a refund, which is

 5   precluded by, inter alia, the Invoice Orders’ statement that “[t]his sale is final, and no refund shall

 6   be issued to Buyer.” (Frimel Decl. Exh. A, ¶ 23; id. Exh. B, ¶ 23.) Epicrew’s declaratory relief

 7   claim merely reiterates the allegations of its other causes of action, and therefore must be

 8   dismissed. See DXC Tech. Co. v. Gen Digital, Inc., No. 23-cv-04818, 2024 WL 2882565, *7

 9   (N.D. Cal. Jun. 7, 2024) (dismissing declaratory relief claim because it “amounts to a backward-

10   looking breach of contract claim”).

11                               ALLEGATIONS OF THE COMPLAINT

12          Epicrew alleges it is based “in Ohmura City, Nagasaki, Japan,” and “is an established and

13   well-known corporation specializing in semiconductor refurbishment services.” (Compl., Dkt.

14   No. 1, ¶ 2.) On May 22, 2023, Epicrew “sent a request to CAE,” i.e., CAET, “for an image of” a

15   “Centura EPI 8 System,” which is equipment related to semiconductor manufacturing, “and its

16   serial number, to which CAE promptly responded stating that it was unable to complete the

17   request at that time because the system was still in operation.” (Id. ¶¶ 1, 11.) The following day,

18   CAET’s David Sardi “sent an invoice for the Centura stating the price as $950,000, plus an

19   estimated price of $15,000 for Settlement Services, bringing the total purchase price to

20   $965,000.” (Id. ¶ 12.) On the same day, Epicrew received another “email from CAE stating, in
21   relevant part,” that “[t]his equipment will be released soon, but it usually takes 3-4 weeks for the

22   supplier to arrange removal. If Epicrew signs before the other offer, our bid of $950K will be

23   accepted. If our second signs, the first buyer will receive the equipment.” (Id. ¶ 13.)

24          On May 24, 2023, Epicrew signed the Invoice Order for the Centura system. (Id. ¶ 14.)

25   The Invoice Order stated, among other things, that “Buyer,” i.e., Epicrew, “agrees not to

26   circumvent CAET by purchasing Equipment directly from CAET’s supplier” (Frimel Decl. Exh.
27   A, ¶ 4); “[a]ll Equipment is offered to Buyer based on its prior sale to CAET,” and “[s]hould such

15

16

17
     17200. . . . Alternatively, a plaintiff may plead that defendants’ conduct is ‘unfair’ within the
18
     meaning of the several standards developed by the courts. . . . Finally, a plaintiff may challenge
19
     ‘fraudulent’ conduct by showing that ‘members of the public are likely to be deceived’ by the
20

21

22

23

24

25
     522 F. Supp. 3d 634, 643 (N.D. Cal. 2021). “Plaintiff’s UCL claim under the ‘fraudulent’ prong
26
     is governed by the pleading requirements of Rule 9.” In re Outlaw Lab., LLP, 463 F. Supp. 3d
27
     1068, 1088 (S.D. Cal. 2020). This theory does not meet Rule 9’s requirements.
